verdict.probe_answer: Both arms' hung-turn test (watchdog_cancels_a_hung_turn_as_timed_out) is the strongest in each: it gates the fake agent forever, sets a 50ms hard_wall_clock, and would hang past the test's own 2s bound on pre-Task5 code (no watchdog wiring) — it asserts the exact Err(AgentTimedOut) variant, that session/cancel was sent, and stream termination. Real behavior, not trivial. The active/unmodeled test in both arms is solid too: it would fail a naive/buggy Task5 implementation that mis-applies FIX-5 saturating idle math or forgets to bump activity on unmodeled (Thought) updates, since idle_timeout(100ms) < total runtime. Weakest in both arms is no_watchdog_config_is_byte_identical, since with watchdog=None nothing computes a deadline, so it can only catch 'over-eager' bugs, not omissions — but Arm A's version is more rigorous: after the 300ms no-timeout check it releases the gate and asserts the turn completes normally with Done{end_turn}, actually verifying 'byte-identical' end-to-end. Arm B's equivalent only checks the 150ms non-response window and rec.cancels being empty, then ends the test without ever releasing the gate or confirming eventual normal completion — a real (if minor) rigor gap, not present in Arm A.
verdict.rationale: Both diffs implement the exact same PFIX-F/G/H/L mechanics: watchdog arm unconditionally discards the inner cancel-select outcome and sets timed_out_local=true+Err(()); the disabled path uses Some/None matched against a pending::<()> future so no task spawns and the arm never fires; sleep_until uses Instant::from_std; la_instant uses saturating_sub(1) undoing the sentinel; drop(done_tx) runs at the common post-select cleanup on every exit path; the terminal match guards Err(()) if timed_out_local before the generic AgentCrashed arm, and Ok(resp) is never relabeled. No WRONG (provably incorrect) behavior found in either — differences are SMELL-level style choices (Arm A: shared la_instant closure, ScriptedUpdate::Sleep enum variant; Arm B: inline duplicated la_instant calc, Recorder-level delay flag). The one concrete test gap is Arm B's byte-identical test never releasing the gate to confirm eventual normal completion, unlike Arm A's version — enough to call A's tests marginally stronger, not enough to call the overall submission materially better since production code correctness is a tie.
